title: Crescent Hotel preps for paranormal lockdown | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
excerpt: Tickets are now on sale for the annual Crescent Hotel Lockdown at the 1886 Crescent Hotel & Spa, 5 Prospect Ave., Eureka Springs, in January.
content:
Tickets are now on sale for the annual Crescent Hotel Lockdown at the 1886 Crescent Hotel & Spa, 5 Prospect Ave., Eureka Springs, in January.

"We like to encourage people to buy them as Christmas gifts," says Debra Workman, the hotel's director of ghost tours and ghost tour supervisor.

On Jan. 5, the hotel will close to the public and as many as 60 holders of tickets ($175 each) will get a chance to explore it between 8 p.m. and 3 a.m.

"All of my guides will be there, on the floors helping guests use equipment and hunt for those spirits," Workman says. "They can go anywhere in the hotel, from the fourth floor all the way down to the morgue.

"They get to hunt for ghosts in the hotel that's completely dark, except for a few little candlelight areas."

The Crescent rooms most associated with paranormal activity -- the ones where guests have reported unexplained noises, moving furniture and strange smells -- will be unlocked and open for exploration.

Lockdown participants will stay at the Basin Hotel -- accommodations are not included in the ticket price; rooms start at $149 -- less than a mile away from the Crescent, with shuttle transportation to and from.

The 16th annual Eureka Springs Paranormal Weekend will be Jan. 29-30, and will offer another extended opportunity for ghost hunters to explore the hotel. The two-day conference fee is $250 per person, and early arrivals can add an overnight ghost investigation experience on Jan. 28.

"We offer workshops on a variety of topics and then they get to hunt every evening," Workman explains.

The Crescent Hotel, built in 1886 as a luxury resort, transitioned into Crescent College in 1902. In 1937, it was bought by Norman Baker, who with no medical training converted it into a hospital promising a cure to cancer.

Baker was convicted of mail fraud in 1940, but not before hundreds of patients died after receiving fake cancer treatments, including watermelon seeds, clover and carbolic acid. The building was damaged in a fire, blamed on faulty wiring, in 1967.

The hotel, which has since been restored and reopened, hosts regular ghost hunts throughout the year, though Workman says those are more limited in scope than the lockdown and ESP events.

Tours for kids 5-12 (must be accompanied by a guardian 18 or older) are $15 for 45 minutes. There are regular, family-friendly ghost tours ($29.50 for 60 minutes), as well as expert and extended tours ($35 for 90 minutes), led by senior paranormal guides each night at 10 p.m. There are also midnight investigations, held only on select occasions, led by seasoned investigators from the Eureka Springs Paranormal Team.

More information on the hotel is available online. This website offers more information on the ghost tours. Make reservations for the lockdown or the ESP Weekend by phone at (855) 725-5720.
